content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a report evaluating the cost-effectiveness of implementing an indeterminate range for early infant diagnosis of HIV. The publication is intended to provide transparency and information, as required by WHO guidelines. HIV remains a significant cause of illness and death among infants and children, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Historically, mother-to-child transmission of HIV was difficult to control in these settings. However, the advent of highly active antiretroviral therapy (ART) and its increased availability and affordability have led to substantial progress in preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. As a result, transmission rates have steadily declined and are expected to continue decreasing with the global scale-up of PMTCT programs. Despite these advancements, unintended challenges have emerged. The accuracy of HIV diagnostic tests, particularly their positive predictive value, is closely tied to the prevalence of HIV among exposed infants. As transmission rates decrease, the likelihood of false-positive test results increases. To address this, WHO recommends that all positive HIV test results be confirmed with a second test. However, in many regions, such as sub-Saharan Africa, confirmatory testing is not routinely performed, with rates as low as 10-15%. Consequently, some HIV-uninfected infants may be erroneously started on lifelong ART without confirmatory testing. To minimize false-positive diagnoses and the associated unnecessary ART regimens, it may be possible to identify test results that are more likely to be false positives. A positive result is reported if the DNA level surpasses a control threshold during a specific cycle, known as the cycle threshold (Ct). In true HIV-positive samples, Ct values are inversely correlated with the amount of HIV DNA present (i.e., a high Ct value corresponds to a low viral load). False-positive results, often due to contamination or technical errors, are typically associated with high Ct values. Therefore, Ct values may help distinguish between true-positive and false-positive results, especially when confirmatory testing is unavailable. This analysis explores the potential benefits, clinical trade-offs, and cost savings of adopting an indeterminate range of Ct values for initial HIV diagnostic tests in settings where confirmatory testing is not routinely performed. The findings suggest that using an indeterminate range could significantly reduce the number of unnecessary ART regimens prescribed. This approach becomes increasingly favorable as PMTCT programs expand globally. Additionally, the indeterminate range could help prioritize infants for confirmatory testing, further improving outcomes. The study modeled the outcomes of 10,000 HIV-exposed infants in sub-Saharan Africa under two diagnostic and treatment algorithms: the standard of care (SoC) and an indeterminate range algorithm based on Ct values. All infants received an initial NAAT for HIV diagnosis within six weeks of birth. Under the SoC, any non-negative test result (positive or indeterminate) led to presumptive ART initiation, with confirmatory testing performed in some cases. Infants with negative confirmatory results discontinued ART, while those with non-negative confirmatory results remained on lifelong ART. In contrast, the indeterminate range algorithm withheld presumptive ART for infants with indeterminate results (high Ct values) until confirmatory testing confirmed a non-negative result. Infants with indeterminate results who did not undergo confirmatory testing did not receive ART. The analysis accounted for the probability of follow-up testing, infant mortality rates, and the costs of testing and treatment. HIV-infected infants receiving ART experienced moderately elevated two-year mortality rates, while those not receiving ART had significantly higher mortality. HIV-uninfected infants erroneously started on ART continued lifelong treatment. The results demonstrated that adopting an indeterminate range could avert a substantial number of unnecessary ART regimens for HIV-uninfected infants, with relatively few additional HIV-related deaths among infected infants. The trade-off between unnecessary ART and excess deaths varied depending on the Ct cutoff used to define the indeterminate range. Lower Ct cutoffs reduced unnecessary ART but increased the risk of missed HIV cases. Prioritizing confirmatory testing for infants with indeterminate results further improved the clinical trade-offs, making the approach even more favorable. In low-prevalence settings, the indeterminate range algorithm was particularly effective, with a clinical trade-off of approximately 24 unnecessary ART regimens averted per excess HIV-related death. When confirmatory testing was prioritized for likely false-positive results, the trade-off improved to 320 unnecessary ART regimens averted per excess death. These findings suggest that, in the absence of widespread confirmatory testing, the use of an indeterminate range can enhance the efficiency of pediatric HIV diagnosis and treatment programs while minimizing adverse clinical consequences.
